item.content:encoded:
The US makes only 60 to 65 missiles a month, and 803 were fired on the first day of the Middle East war. Zelensky says what Putin wants is a long war, because running out of resources hurts Ukraine.

Medium information density, but Zelensky gives several concrete numbers and judgments, more substantive than a press release. The second half, about his personal life and family, can be fast-forwarded.

0:02 The Middle East war directly drains Ukraine's air defense missiles
Zelensky says the Middle East war's impact on Ukraine is direct: a global fuel shortage and, more importantly, air defense missile supply being squeezed. He states plainly that "there will be a reduced number of missiles for our defense." He is already looking for alternatives, because Ukraine ran short of anti-missile missiles this past winter, and the next winter is still coming. He also says the US diplomatic focus is now on the Middle East, and trilateral talks keep getting postponed for one reason only: the Iran war.

4:04 What Putin wants is exactly a long war
Zelensky's judgment is that for Putin, a long war in Iran is a plus. The reason is not just energy prices, but that it consumes US stockpiles and the production capacity of air defense missile makers. When the US needs extra resources it turns to Europe, and Europe as an ally gives them. The result is that resources do not flow to Ukraine. Zelensky says Putin needs to weaken Ukraine, and the Middle East is one of the ways to do that.

5:05 The US makes a month's worth of missiles; the Middle East burns them in a day
Zelensky gives a set of concrete numbers: the US produces 60 to 65 missiles a month, roughly 700 to 800 a year. On the first day of the Middle East war, 803 were used. He says Middle Eastern countries used PAC-3 to intercept drones early in the war, because PAC-3 can hit any aerial target. The question now is when Middle East stockpiles run out. His conclusion: Ukraine will certainly face a missile shortage.

6:07 What Ukraine wants is production licenses, not sympathy
Zelensky's demands of Western leaders are specific: unity first, speed second. He says the war made Ukraine number one in military technology, not because it is smarter, but because it has underground manufacturers. What he wants is for European friends to give Ukraine's industrial sector the maximum licenses, rights and opportunities so Ukraine can produce the weapons it lacks itself. He says this is Ukraine's first interest.

9:12 Trump wants to end the war but does not want to pick a side
Zelensky says he believes Trump genuinely wants to end the war, because Trump promised voters and wants to finish quickly. But Trump's strategy is to keep close dialogue with Putin and not provoke him, while not fully siding with Ukraine. Zelensky says Trump positions himself as a mediator, not on either side. Ukraine wants Trump on Ukraine's side, because the more countries stand with Ukraine, the more pressure on Russia. But the US has its own strategy.

12:27 Putin is not ready to sign any agreement, only to dictate an ultimatum
Zelensky says Putin is not ready to sign any agreement; what he wants is for Ukraine to sign an ultimatum. Putin understands that giving up the Donbas means splitting Ukrainian society, and a split society can be exploited. Zelensky says Putin's goal is division, because a divided country is a weak country that can be occupied further. He says Ukraine is ready to compromise, especially if the US is involved, but the US has not demanded major compromises from Russia.

14:30 Be as fair to the Russian regime as to Iran
Zelensky says the West must be fair toward different regimes. If there is a certain attitude toward Maduro or the Iranian regime, the same attitude should apply to the Russian regime, because they are no different on human rights, freedom or nuclear threats. He says the first step should be a diplomatic solution, but in a tough way that gives Putin the same terms as other regimes. He states plainly that toppling the regime is step two; step one is diplomacy.

20:36 If Ukraine joins NATO, the war is over
Zelensky reiterates that he is willing to give up his position if it buys NATO membership. He says if NATO recognizes Ukraine's army as one of Europe's strongest, he is willing to consider his work done. He says if Ukraine were in NATO, the war would be over. He also says he does not think there is a big problem in the relationship between Trump and Starmer, and that history is stronger than the emotions of two or three people.

item.title: America's richest aren't CEOs — they own car washes and HVAC companies
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-mastersinbiz-美国最富的一群人-不是ceo而是开洗车店和暖通公司的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-mastersinbiz-美国最富的一群人-不是ceo而是开洗车店和暖通公司的/
item.description: Three million private business owners in the US hold net worth above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies and car dealerships, and they got there by owning, not by earning a salary.
item.content:encoded:
Three million private business owners in the US hold net worth above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies and car dealerships, and they got there by owning, not by earning a salary.

The data comes from IRS and Treasury tax records, finer-grained than the Fed's surveys. The core conclusion: to reach the top 0.1%, own a business rather than earn a high salary.

1:03 The IRS asked them to audit taxes and they accidentally built a wealth database
Both authors were recruited straight out of graduate school by the Treasury Department and the Office of Tax Analysis to solve a tax-policy puzzle: pass-through businesses don't pay tax themselves, so you have to link the business back to its individual owner to compute the tax burden. The project accidentally produced a panel database that tracks every business along with its owners and employees — far richer than the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances, which is large in scale but nowhere near as granular as tax records.

3:08 Wealth isn't in Silicon Valley or Wall Street — the whole map lights up
The authors assumed wealth was concentrated in tech and finance, and the data overturned that bias. When they plotted the "everywhere millionaire" on a map, the entire country lit up. These rich people are spread across a large number of unsexy industries — car dealerships, HVAC, dental practices, restaurants, distribution, sanitation. It isn't only the Forbes 400 getting richer; it's millions of people.

4:08 Three million private business owners hold ten times the wealth of the Forbes 400
The authors counted roughly 3 million "everywhere millionaires" — private business owners with net worth of at least $5 million. Their combined wealth is more than ten times the total of the Forbes 400. That number changes the inequality narrative: what drives inequality statistics is not a few hundred billionaires but millions of unknown business owners.

8:10 The higher the income, the smaller the wage share and the larger the business share
Break open the top 10% of earners: people at the 90th percentile live mainly on wages. But moving up, the curves cross — by the top 0.1%, most income comes from business income. The authors say the main typical way to get rich in America is to own something, not to earn a wage. That is both a tax advantage (owning is taxed more lightly than earning a wage) and the actual path of wealth accumulation.

10:15 The 1986 tax reform turned pass-through from a disadvantage into an advantage
The 1986 tax reform (Reagan as president, Democrats controlling Congress, a bipartisan effort) lowered the individual income tax rate below the corporate rate for the first time. Before that, pass-through was unattractive because of its tax disadvantage; afterward, being a pass-through became cheaper. The Bush tax cuts later lowered individual rates further, and the 2017 tax reform added a 20% deduction for certain pass-through categories. The result: more than half of business income is pass-through income, nearly half of employment is at pass-through businesses, and almost all small businesses are pass-throughs.

13:18 Half of the top 1%'s income growth came from pass-through
The authors ran a counterfactual: if you held fixed the importance of pass-through business income as of 1985 (before the 1986 tax reform) and let it develop as it was, roughly half of the top 1%'s income growth would disappear. Looking at wealth growth, from 1989 to the latest SCF data, two-thirds of the top 0.1%'s wealth growth came from private businesses. This shows pass-through is absolutely central, in accounting terms, to the growth of wealth and top-end income.

14:20 Entrepreneurs earn only about 10% more on average, but failure isn't the end
Using data tracking roughly 10 million entrepreneurship events since 2000, the authors found that founders earn about 10% more on average than similar workers who didn't start a business — and that's before counting unrealized capital gains from selling the business, and the average already includes a large number of failures. About 20% of founders are serial entrepreneurs — it's the second or third venture that actually earns the yacht money. After a failure you can return to the labor market or start again and fix what went wrong last time.

19:27 Every congressional district has a millionaire business owner
The authors say "every congressional district has an everywhere millionaire." Unlike Silicon Valley and Wall Street, which are concentrated in specific geographies, almost every district has a car dealer. These business owners employ many people, pay a lot of sales tax and are prominent in their local communities, so they wield a lot of influence — their approval ratings are higher than those of the military, the Supreme Court and Congress. About a quarter of members of Congress are private business owners; count law-firm partners and that share can reach 40% to 50%. At the state and local level, because the positions are part-time and low-paid, business owners make up an even larger share — mayors especially.

item.title: AI can now build a virus; the defense side is still stuck on sequence alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.description: The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline still stuck at sequence matching.
item.content:encoded:
The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline still stuck at sequence matching.

High information density; the middle and later sections on the four layers of biodefense, the DNA synthesis pipeline, and "you can't patch a human" are the most valuable.

0:00 The teams doing design are best positioned to do defense
The dual mission Eric set for Radical Numerics is not a PR gesture but a technical judgment: the models that can generate pathogenic sequences and the models that can tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models. So the teams doing design are naturally best positioned to do defense, rather than outsourcing defense to a different group. He acknowledges there is an arms-race dynamic here, and that the defense side has always been far behind; what the company wants to do is pull the defense side up to the same level.

8:12 AI built the first genome from scratch
Evo's work generating a CRISPR-Cas system landed in Science, and Eric later gave a TED Talk. More important is what scientists showed last year: using a generative DNA model to generate the first genome from scratch. Humans had previously only been able to copy and paste fragments of known function, and had never built from scratch at the genome level. What Evo generated was a functional bacteriophage, that is, a virus. Eric says this is a turning point for the scientific community and the company — it means being able to build complete organisms that do not exist in nature, and it also means the corresponding potential for harm.

12:16 Omni's breakthrough came from alignment, not pretraining
Evo showed the potential of pretraining, but on human genetics it still lost to specialized DNA models, and the community questioned why large models were needed at all. Omni's difference lies in midtraining and posttraining: presenting tasks in the question-and-answer form scientists actually want, for example, given a wild-type and a mutant sequence, help me find the causal variant. Eric says this kind of form does not emerge naturally from pretraining. The results surprised them — Omni was not just competitive across many tasks the way Evo was, it began pushing the frontier in every subfield, especially variant effect prediction.

23:50 Most real disease variants are in non-coding regions
Traditional bioinformatics tools and statistical methods mainly focus on coding regions, and coding regions make up only about 1.5% to 2% of the genome. Eric says many, perhaps most, diseases actually fall in non-coding regulatory regions, where variants are harder to judge as pathogenic or not. This is exactly where Omni is strong: it can distinguish pathogenic mutations in non-coding regions, especially long-range ones. This is exactly what geneticists who have long been unable to use traditional tools want.

45:44 The biology experiment itself is doing the filtering
The mechanism of the SOLEX experiment is worth remembering: generate a large number of random sequences, turn them into aptamer switches, and read them out at high throughput with NGS — the more binding, the more reads, the higher the fitness; then mutate the winning sequences again and iterate. This experiment explored on the order of 10 to the 11th power sequences in parallel. The key is that "the biology of the experiment is actually doing the filtering" — the wet lab does the filtering, and the model reproduces that process in silico. This paradigm can be generalized to any biological experiment of "progressive refinement," as long as you can capture the intermediate states.

58:15 Stanford scientists said generating DNA was a stupid idea
Eric spent six months at Stanford on the idea of Evo "generating DNA," and almost every scientist he talked to thought it was a stupid idea. The objections were specific: humans themselves do not understand the rules of DNA, so why expect AI to learn them; you cannot even tell whether the generation is correct, so how do you give the model feedback; DNA has too many repetitive sequences, too noisy a distribution, no real rules, all junk. He admits he was just stubborn, felt "it just feels right," but at the time could not say what the use case was. The first time they trained Evo, they had no idea whether it would work.

1:12:48 The four pillars of biodefense
They break biodefense into four layers: detection and surveillance (detecting pathogen sequences from environmental samples such as airport nasal swabs and wastewater systems), attribution (judging whether the source is natural, foreign, or engineered in some country's lab), countermeasures (making antivirals or antibacterials), and deterrence (at the government level). They focus on the first three. The core criticism is this: the existing biodefense community mainly relies on sequence matching — aligning sequences against databases of known pathogens. This does not stop two things: new things that are not in the database, and designs that are deliberately obfuscated, that do not match in sequence space but have the same function.

1:25:15 You can't patch a human
The host points out the key difference between biosecurity and cybersecurity: in cybersecurity, a sufficiently strong model can in principle find every vulnerability and patch it, and as long as people keep updating, they are safe; but the genome is fixed, "you can't patch a human," so the defense surface is harder. Conversely there are two buffers: the intensity of motivation to launch an attack may be much lower, and the threshold from printing arbitrary DNA to building a successful virus — especially one that does not first kill the designer — is actually quite high.

item.title: Whose Homes Did His Roads Tear Down: Robert Moses's New York Legacy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-stuffmissed-他修的路拆了谁的房-罗伯特-摩西的纽约遗产/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-stuffmissed-他修的路拆了谁的房-罗伯特-摩西的纽约遗产/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Moses used federal Title I money to tear down 26 neighborhoods, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees were better housed — his legacy remains unresolved to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Moses used federal Title I money to tear down 26 neighborhoods, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees were better housed — his legacy remains unresolved to this day.

This episode has medium information density, but the second half is worth hearing for its details on how power operates, media manipulation, and the mechanics of urban renewal; the first half can be fast-forwarded.

2:03 The more power, the less explanation needed
After LaGuardia retired in 1946, William O'Dwyer appointed Moses as New York City Construction Coordinator, a position that gave him jurisdiction over every public construction project in the city and a direct line to Washington. By 1959, critics pointed out that he simultaneously held multiple government positions and his power was unchecked: consultant fees were not public, staff salaries were not public, trust meetings were held behind closed doors, and he could seize land at will. Reporter Bob Baum noted that private companies could do these things, but as part of a government entity, the public had a right to know. Moses was therefore often called the "Construction Czar" or "Urban Planning Czar."

3:07 Roads first, at the cost of entire communities
In 1948, Moses began building the Cross Bronx Expressway, a seven-mile road cutting through the already heavily developed Bronx. Dozens of apartment buildings were demolished, hundreds of families were displaced, and many streets were cut into dead ends. This community fragmentation was later cited as one reason for rising local crime rates. Those affected were mostly the least resourced, predominantly non-white communities. In a 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, Moses wrote that arterial improvements were "not merely a strip of pavement laid in a gasoline ditch, but a real improvement of the entire area." He genuinely believed he was making the best choices for New York, but his methods were often ruthless.

7:12 26 brochures, one visual persuasion campaign
In 1949, Congress passed the American Housing Act Title I, providing $1 billion in loans and $100 million in annual grants for slum clearance. Moses realized New York could get a large amount of federal money, so in the 1950s he had his team produce 26 brochures, each targeting a neighborhood he thought needed redevelopment. The brochures contained problem descriptions, photos, and statistics, and were sent to the New York City Board of Estimate, the City Planning Commission, the Title I federal administrator, and the Housing and Home Finance Agency. In 2014, researcher Temis Kronopoulos analyzed the photos and found: vacant lots were shown 22 times, the most common image of urban decay; 20 photos showed back-alley garbage and clotheslines; almost no people appeared in the photos. Kronopoulos wrote: "In this context, slum clearance was also a tool of social engineering."

10:18 Media praise first, scandal exposed later
On June 29, 1959, New York Times reporter Wayne Phillips began publishing a four-part series exposing problems in Moses's Title I slum clearance projects: associations with people he shouldn't have been involved with, unregulated funds, and information not shared. But as early as June 14, columns by George Sokolski began appearing in multiple newspapers nationwide, syndicated by King Features Syndicate, with titles like "Robert Moses Is a Selfless Man" and nearly identical content, praising him for "constantly building and beautifying, his work never tainted by corruption." These articles appeared two weeks before the New York Times critical series. Looking back, Sokolski appears to have been asked to preemptively cover for the coming scandal.

13:22 Mayor's ban and public tantrum
After the scandal broke, Mayor Wagner did two things: first, he investigated Louis Pokras's role in the Harlem slum clearance project, and because Pokras had organized crime connections, Wagner publicly stated he would never allow him to sponsor any New York development project; second, he banned the city government from working with Moses's favored architect Melvin E. Kessler, whose previous involvement in Upper West Side redevelopment saw developer Manhattan Town Incorporated take Title I funds without building a single building or demolishing a single building, just collecting rent while the buildings decayed. Moses publicly responded that the mayor's "devastating charges and misstatements" scared off venture capital, and said "Title I is a dead duck." Other officials said Title I would continue and praised Moses. Looking back at media coverage, Moses appeared to be throwing a public tantrum.

15:26 "Moses Must Go": an open letter
In December 1959, the Metropolitan Housing Council began distributing leaflets in New York addressed to Mayor Robert Wagner. At the top in bold letters: "For New York's development, Moses must go." The leaflet listed ongoing problems with slum clearance projects: tenants were sold along with the land; indecent relocation practices continued; luxury housing was built at the people's expense while those who needed housing most were pushed from one slum to another; as former rent administrator Charles Abrams pointed out, slum clearance had become "Negro and Puerto Rican removal." The leaflet demanded: more low-rent housing, an end to subsidizing luxury housing, and building new housing before demolishing old. It compared the situation to cancer and repeated: "Moses must go."

21:32 Fire Island showdown: Rockefeller accepts the resignation
In 1962, Moses clashed with New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller over the Fire Island road plan. Moses wanted to build a road spanning the entire island, and after a 1962 storm destroyed most houses, he thought his chance had come. But environmental groups and islanders opposed it, and residents proposed an alternative: making Fire Island a national seashore protected area, which gained federal support. Public pressure gave the governor an opportunity to halt the road project and suggest Moses reduce his government roles to focus on the 1964 World's Fair. Moses submitted his resignation; he had previously threatened other governors with resignation, but they had all refused because many public projects would collapse without him. Rockefeller accepted the resignation, triggering a media storm. Moses claimed the governor had asked him to immediately resign as chairman of the State Parks Commission so his brother Lawrence could take over; Rockefeller said a transition had been discussed for over a year.

26:38 World's Fair: 50 million vs. expected 70 million
The 1964 New York World's Fair attracted about 50 million people, but Moses had predicted 70 million. The New York Times reported that only 85% of the grounds were ready at opening, 15 of 139 pavilions were unfinished, and many completed pavilions had no exhibits. Some exhibitors arrived with nowhere to put their displays. A fair spokesman told the media that visiting all the other options would take over a week, and unfinished pavilions would be completed before then. Some attractions were finished within weeks of opening, others were abandoned entirely. After the fair, Moses no longer served as New York City Construction Coordinator. In September 1966, his wife Mary died after a long illness, and less than a month later, Moses remarried Mary Grady, who served as secretary at the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority. In 1968, Rockefeller merged Triborough into another transportation agency, and Moses was removed from his last New York government position.

item.title: Google Hid Its Quantum Recipe. A Bunch of Amateurs Beat It.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-zeroknowledge-google-藏起来的量子方案-被一群业余研究者反超了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-zeroknowledge-google-藏起来的量子方案-被一群业余研究者反超了/
item.description: Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, without publishing the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition where agents build on each other's submissions — and the field beat Google's result by more than 60%.
item.content:encoded:
Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, without publishing the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition where agents build on each other's submissions — and the field beat Google's result by more than 60%.

High information density: it explains the mechanics of an automated-research competition, the verifier design, and several real breakthrough cases. Worth hearing for anyone following AI for science, ZK, and open innovation.

4:07 Google gives the proof, not the circuit
Google published a paper claiming a more resource-efficient quantum approach than the previous state of the art for breaking the secp256k1 elliptic curve — the basis of Bitcoin's and Ethereum's public-key cryptography. But Google did not publish the approach; it used a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate that it does possess such an approach. Soubhik points out the consequence: if you want to prepare for Q-day, you have to know what approaches will appear, how to harden systems, what the defences are; if you don't understand any of that, you are not prepared for Q-day. Not publishing the quantum circuit is the main consequence here.

8:08 The competition is not solo work, it is a relay
ecdsa.fail is not played by everyone doing the work locally and then submitting. The platform backend runs the same verifier Google used; through a command-line interface you have your agent read the competition details and other people's submissions, then build directly on top of someone else's approach. Soubhik says this is how research actually works: you build on each other's experience, not like an Olympic event where everyone submits independently. Anna says she had assumed it was PvP, everyone finishing on their own machine and submitting to compete; Soubhik confirms it is not. This multi-user automated-research framework produced enormous acceleration, because you don't have to rediscover everything yourself.

11:08 Three breakthroughs: externalising, mining, starting over
Soubhik sees three big breakthroughs. The first was externalising the environment and letting people outside the company take part — one team member who had not been involved in internal testing spent roughly $5,000 on a codex subscription the day before internal testing and made a huge jump that the lead engineer could not understand. The second was mining French's work, building on it and surpassing Google's result within two weeks. After that the chart was almost a plateau for two months. The third came in mid-August: Teddy, from Starkware, went back to the starting point of the competition, summarised all the techniques into a knowledge review, and then built from scratch rather than on other people's ideas, ultimately proposing the NSD ping-pong technique, which pushed the approach from 49% better than Google to 57% better, and now past 60%.

27:15 If the question is posed wrong, there is no competition
Soubhik says many problems are posed incorrectly — that is, badly formulated. He gives the example: ‘Build me a quantum computer’ — that problem is too big, we don't know what it is. But if you break it down, you find that the problem state of ecdsa.fail is one of its subproblems. You need to split the big problem into a series of well-formulated subtasks, then run automated research on each subtask. Another example is the proximity gap conjecture: EF committed a $1 million prize, but the original statement is binary — you either prove it or you don't — and it is hard to write a verifier for it. Later Alexander Hicks and Gako wrote a simple verifier for one specific instance of the conjecture, and that is what became the better.codes competition.

39:15 An algebraic geometer broke 64 bits in hours
better.codes has two bounds: the lower bound is the soundness bound, the upper bound is the attack bound. The lower bound had been stuck at the Johnson bound for years. On August 21 the competition was stuck at 63.99 bits, and 64 bits is the Johnson bound for this specific instance. Then there was no progress for 6 days; the chart was a straight line. Until August 28, when the team contacted Bartosz from ECDSA — a Polish mathematician specialising in algebraic geometry, not a cryptographer at all, who had never heard of the problem. Within a few hours of joining he pushed the result from 63.99 to 64.0101 bits, breaking the Johnson bound for the first time. The technique he used was some combination of algebraic geometry, because he had already been using his own codex subscription to do algebraic geometry work, and he probably applied algebraic geometry methods to this problem.

41:15 One breakthrough detonated a 30-year open problem
After Bartosz broke 64.01 bits, the whole circle blew up, with Ariel Gabizon, Kobi and others discussing it on Twitter. The story did not end there: a few days later, some cryptographers had a bigger problem in coding theory that had been open for 30 years — proving a certain soundness bound. Within days three papers appeared claiming inspiration from the method used to break the Johnson bound. Soubhik says nobody could have predicted this; this is open innovation and collaborative research, and it still looks very early: people are starting to realise that problems they thought would not be solved for a long time can at least be pushed forward and improved.

45:18 Domain experts guide agents on GitHub
On the hish tiling problem, Yukon piloted a discussion-format feature. The whole process is in the CLI; you don't even need to think or prompt your agent. While doing research the agent searches for information in the hills and formulates strategies locally, and at the same time uploads discussions to a GitHub forum. Other agents read those discussions, and domain experts like Bartosz answer by hand, and the agents read those answers — so the domain expert is effectively steering the automated-research network. Soubhik says this is exactly what they want: a domain expert should see where the automated-research network has got to on his problem statement, then use his best intuition to steer it and leave clues about what to explore.

52:20 Yukon wants to be an AI-native research institution
Soubhik says Yukon's vision is to grow into an AI-based research institution, imitating three features of traditional research institutions: research means building at a higher level on each other's ideas; the originators of ideas must be credited; and even failed ideas should be recognised, because one success may come out of a thousand failures. What AI changes is that the whole research lifecycle accelerates from months or years to days. They are implementing a partial credit system so people can give each other credit for ideas, including negative credit — failed ideas also earn credit. They also want a system that helps you decompose a badly formulated problem into a series of well-formulated subproblems.

item.title: Information Has Never Been More Abundant, and We Choose Not to Know
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-iq2-信息从未如此充裕-我们却选择不知道/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-iq2-信息从未如此充裕-我们却选择不知道/
item.description: Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years, and her judgment is this: not knowing isn't because there isn't enough information, it's because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice, and it has made everything worse.
item.content:encoded:
Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years, and her judgment is this: not knowing isn't because there isn't enough information, it's because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice, and it has made everything worse.

The first half is instant judgment on Iran and Hormuz; the second half is a rare post-mortem on whether twenty years of intervention in Afghanistan was worth it. High information density, but it demands patience.

3:13 Not knowing is because you don't want to know
Doucet calls this "a really jarring time": information has never been more abundant, but "If we don't know about something, it's because we don't want to know about something. We choose not to know." She traces the cause to being bombarded every day by the US president's statements — yesterday it was "we don't need guardrails on AI," even though some of the leading founders in AI are asking for regulation; today it's rolling back some environmental regulations. She warns: a president who says he won't get into "forever wars" still ends up leading the country into those wars.

5:15 This is a war of choice, and it keeps getting worse
Doucet rarely offers a personal judgment: this war puts her under great pressure, because it is "a war of choice" rather than "a war of necessity," and "it just seems to have made everything worse in every way." She acknowledges that the US and Israel together have done enormous damage to Iran's military and navy, and that Iran's economy is suffering, but strategically "this is a war where President Trump doesn't know how to end it." Iran has not collapsed, the regime is harder than before, the promises made to the demonstrators have not been kept, and their lives have gotten worse instead.

6:16 Daily market life under 82% inflation
Doucet uses inflation to illustrate Iran's predicament: Britons worry about single-digit inflation, "Oh, 4%, oh my God, it's 5%," while Iran is at 82%. She quotes an Iranian woman: I come to the market every day just to watch the prices go up, that's how I pass the time. She then sets Iran alongside Ukraine — both are "war of choice" and miscalculation; Trump thought he could drive straight through Iran, Putin thought he could drive straight through Ukraine, and both found that people's resistance is both creative and determined.

8:16 Iran has weaponized the Strait of Hormuz
Doucet gives the concrete mechanism: the Houthis control the western shore of the Red Sea and the islands in between, claiming they don't affect maritime traffic, but the previously de-escalating war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen has reignited; oil has risen past $108 a barrel; the Strait of Hormuz is completely frozen. The Iranians won't let go — they don't treat it merely as a bargaining chip but as a long-term chip, "They've weaponized the Strait of Hormuz." She notes that Trump repeatedly says "I didn't expect them to do this," but anyone who has done war-gaming will tell you the games always move quickly toward Iran controlling Hormuz.

40:12 A "traditional Afghanistan" denied by exiles
When the Taliban required Afghan women to wear a burqa that leaves only the eyes exposed, Afghan women abroad pushed back, saying this is not traditional Afghanistan. Doucet points out that the burqa is locally called a chadili, with an embroidered mesh; but in the same period women were also being educated at Kabul University. While writing her book she dug out a large number of old photographs and decided she had to tell this history well, so she tracked down a person living in the United States — whose first reaction was "The Intercontinental, I love that hotel." Their first call lasted four hours, and the person drew the hotel's ground-floor plan from memory, pointing out which room belonged to the German wife of the mayor of Kabul and which to an Indian.

41:12 Four hours of oral history, six months of silence
The second call lasted three hours, after which the person disappeared for about six months. The reason lay in Afghanistan's politics: in '73 the kingdom was ended by the first coup, and hotel employees were taken away for questioning — "Why do you work for an American hotel? Are you working for the CIA?" In '78 came the communist coup, people were thrown into prison, and she could only flee. Happy memories thus turned up sadness and pain. In the end Doucet called to ask for permission, and the person said: I can't appear in your book, it's too sad and too painful for me. Doucet's conclusion: a person writing a book can only get up the next day and find someone else to tell the story, and it will never be told as well.

1:03:14 Two trillion dollars bought a generation that knows its rights
Confronted with the question of what it was all for, Doucet acknowledges that both sides made mistakes, that this should be a humbling lesson for all NATO allies, and that there will be a formal reckoning. But she insists it was not wasted: twenty years of international involvement created the space for the most educated and most connected generation in Afghanistan's history to grow up. She quotes Malala Yousafzai — even reading a book is an act of resistance — and says these girls know their rights, know that Islam gave them the right to education, know that girls around the world go to school while they cannot. "Not enough, but it's not zero."

1:14:42 The difference between hope and optimism is agency
Doucet says she could never tell hope and optimism apart until she read Gordon Brown's "The Future Starts With Us": optimism is wishful thinking, whereas hope is different because hope carries agency — you don't just make a wish, you actually work to bring it about. She says she doesn't have the privilege of "not needing to have hope"; the agency she has is fighting for an Afghan visa, listening to stories there, and telling those stories as well as she can; and everyone has their own bit of agency — some donate money, some help girls take classes online, some teach girls in Africa, some help South Sudan, Nicaragua, and some help struggling areas within Britain itself.

item.title: Russia Won't Invade NATO, But It Is Testing Whether NATO Holds Together
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.description: Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey-zone ambiguity to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey-zone ambiguity to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.

The first half, on Russian hybrid warfare and NATO cohesion, is very dense; the Middle East section in the second half wanders somewhat, but the detail about Houthis using Claude to improve their missiles is worth hearing.

4:30 No ground-invasion risk, but hybrid escalation is rising
Joshi says it plainly: there is no risk of a Russian conventional ground offensive against NATO, this is not the kind of alarm it was in January 2022. The entire security apparatus of Estonia and Finland exists to detect exactly that kind of movement, and every port, naval base and forest route in western Russia is blanketed with intelligence and technical sensors. But another risk is rising: Russia's tolerance for hybrid operations below the Article V threshold is increasing. They have already used drones against Ukrainian cargo planes that might be bound for Ukraine, planted explosives in DHL parcels in Leipzig, and sabotaged power plants and railways across Europe. The question is: would they actually fire missiles at Polish facilities? Joshi thinks Russia is still quite cautious and wants to avoid dragging NATO into a broader conflict, but that debate is unresolved in Europe.

10:15 Poland sounds the loudest alarm; the Baltics say things are fine
The most alarming signal this week came from Poland. Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia might attack Poland and other NATO allies — not a conventional ground attack, but drones and missiles landing on NATO territory that Russia could portray as accidents. But Latvia's leadership, including the defence minister and the president, said there is no reason to panic and no elevated operational risk. Estonia also said it sees no risk of Russia aggressing in that way. Joshi says he has spoken to intelligence officials in multiple countries and sees no reason to fear a ground offensive. The disagreement is itself the signal: Poland is raising the alarm, the Baltic states are cooling things down, and Russia is watching who believes whom.

14:20 Russia's real goal is to corrode NATO cohesion
Joshi lays out Russia's political objective: not to conquer NATO territory or occupy Western Europe, but to weaken and break apart NATO's unity. The mechanism works like this: if a drone lands on Polish territory and blows up a warehouse, Russia says it was an accident, and then Trump says ‘I spoke to Putin and he assured me it was an accident’ — and that lays the alliance's internal divisions bare. Under the Biden administration, Jake Sullivan would call the Russians and say that if this continues you are risking us joining the war on Ukraine's side, and we will retaliate. But under a Trump administration, does Russia really believe Trump would step into a crisis the same way? So Russia has an opportunity not only to push back against attacks on Russia, but to test NATO's cohesion and its boundaries.

19:40 On Ukraine, Trump criticises in public and supplies intelligence in private
Joshi says Trump's support for Ukraine is quite limited, far below the Biden era. The US has effectively let weapons aid lapse; Ukraine desperately needs Patriot interceptor missiles, but because the US has burned through so much in the Iran war, it has given Ukraine almost no interceptors recently. Diplomatically, the administration leans toward Russia and expects Ukraine to make concessions. But there are two exceptions: first, the new Graham bill, which the president has agreed to, would impose new sanctions on Russian entities and force Trump to levy tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and do not reduce their purchases — in practice China and India, and possibly Central European countries. Second, Trump is quietly, not publicly, providing intelligence to Ukraine to help it strike Russian energy facilities. That is the strange reversal: Trump criticises Ukraine overall, but secret assistance is still happening.

26:10 The Strait of Hormuz is still half-closed
The Trump administration insists this is not a war; Trump calls it an ‘excursion’. But the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, and oil traffic is far below pre-war levels. There is no deal with Iran, no resolution. Iran's nuclear programme has no formal limits, and there is no formal commitment to reopen Hormuz. Trump faces the midterms in a month and desperately needs to avoid a sharp escalation of the war that sends oil prices soaring. But politically he cannot make the concessions to Iran that a deal would require, because that would be too humiliating, too obviously equivalent to defeat, and would look catastrophic before an election. So it is a stalemate: Iran has considerable control over the strait, with occasional clashes — the US bombs Iranian coastal missile bases, Iran strikes tankers trying to pass through Hormuz.

31:45 Houthis used Claude to improve their ballistic missiles
Joshi tells a striking detail: when Anthropic published its report on harmful uses of Claude, one of the examples was Houthis using Claude to improve their ballistic missile programme. This group, widely seen as technologically primitive, is using the most advanced AI on Earth to improve the guidance systems of the ballistic missiles they fire at shipping in the Middle East. Mounk adds that being able — at least until being cut off — to access the most advanced American technology to strike America and America's allies is itself a fascinating story. This connects the Ukraine and Russia discussion to the Houthi discussion: in modern war, defensive capability dominates on the ground, but offensive capability dominates in the air.

38:20 Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield
Joshi offers a unifying framework for why ground defence dominates while air strikes still work: it is all about perception. To hit something, you first need to perceive it — find it on the battlefield, then fire at it. That is much harder than it sounds. Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield; actually firing is secondary. On the Ukrainian front line, this is a sensor-saturated environment: small drones everywhere, thermal cameras detecting movement at night, radar seeing through foliage, satellites targeting the area. Anything that moves gets hit — it is a kill zone. But you cannot perceive everywhere equally easily. Drones can see ten kilometres behind the battlefield, but fifty kilometres back, satellite coverage is patchy. It is like the fog of war in a real-time strategy game — you send units out and the fog clears, but where you have not been remains fog. That is why Iran can still launch ballistic missiles, and why Houthis can fire from the mountains of Yemen into the Red Sea.

item.title: The young are useful to society as heretics, not as good citizens
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-a16z-年轻人对社会的用处是当异端-不是当好公民/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-a16z-年轻人对社会的用处是当异端-不是当好公民/
item.description: Universities train young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects, they just need to be allowed to.
item.content:encoded:
Universities train young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects, they just need to be allowed to.

Medium information density, but Amjad's path from chess to training models to building new Replit products is very concrete, and useful for judging whether young people should start companies now.

4:07 The young are useful as heretics
Amjad uses the sci-fi novel The City and the Stars as an analogy: in that city governed by an AGI, everyone is repeatedly reborn from compressed memories, until the machine breaks down and a genuinely new person is born, who immediately starts asking ‘what is outside the walls’. Amjad says the young are useful precisely for asking that kind of question, for being heretics. But today's universities do the opposite — they tell you ‘we have already figured everything out, just learn our way’, and train you into a good citizen: marry, have kids, buy a house, buy a car. The problem is that world no longer exists; you can perform brilliantly in college and still end up unemployed with a pile of debt.

5:11 Silicon Valley is itself a monoculture
Amjad says every society has blind spots, and Silicon Valley has plenty — it is a monoculture, with a fixed way of thinking, so many ideas simply will never grow out of Silicon Valley. Even the most radical culture is, at bottom, a monoculture. So you need young people to experiment, to attempt what is considered impossible, and occasionally someone breaks through: impossible yesterday, suddenly possible today because the technology changed. What universities should do is gather clear-minded, first-principles thinkers and encourage them to question the things that are deeply believed.

15:33 Raising money at 18 is an overused option
Gagan says young people today face a deeply unfair binary: either go to a four-year university and be governed by attendance, homework, exams and grades, or tomorrow someone hands you $50,000 to start a company. He thinks the investor path should be used far less, and only a very small number of teenagers should raise money. Most people at 17 or 18 know they want to enter the business world, but having two years to explore and learn without pressure is precious. He argues for a middle ground: two years to explore freely, with Silicon Valley actively sending information and resources your way, and more support if you have a good idea.

17:35 Starting too early is premature optimization
Amjad borrows a phrase from programming, ‘premature optimization is the root of all evil’: a lot of founding is premature optimization. He sees many kids now inside a circle where friends are raising big rounds and some have become unicorns, so the motive becomes a negative one like envy, and then they pre-commit to an idea they are not even interested in, optimizing in advance for a path they have not yet reached. He says the real question is what your curiosity is driving you toward; once you find the idea you are willing to spend ten years, a lifetime, on, it has enormous gravity and you cannot dodge it — he himself actively did not want to start a company, but the thing blew up into one on its own. He also says VCs now go to Stanford and give students a million dollars with no idea yet, so they have a cap table before they have even started, which is a bit like the music industry signing young artists.

20:43 From chess all the way to training models
Amjad says he has always swung between ‘wanting to build things’ and ‘wanting to read and explore widely’, the two feeding each other in a recursive process. He gives his recent obsession with chess as an example: he started playing very late, does not know why he was interested, then began writing programs to solve chess and training models, and found that LLMs are terrible at chess and hallucinate moves that do not exist. To figure it out, he — who had never trained a model — spent a lot of time studying how to train one. He realized from this that AI can now do machine learning itself, just as in 2024 Replit's agent suddenly learned to write code and afterward coding changed completely; machine learning may be at that same moment — he calls it vibe research or auto research. He is now building products at Replit to let anyone become a machine learning researcher, or let a boss with data fine-tune a model to solve a specific problem.

23:46 Companies will become self-driving organizations
Amjad thinks the shape of companies will change. Silicon Valley has tried many experiments to remake companies — Holacracy, Medium tried it, GitHub tried a no-manager system, all failed spectacularly — but he thinks that was a technology problem: now you can let agents act as the connective tissue of an organization, turn bureaucratic processes into invisible things machines do in the background, give people real autonomy to work on what interests them most, and have AI judge your impact. He says he has already changed how management works at Replit, calls it a ‘self-driving company’, and that ultimately the company will run itself. He admits he does not have a fully formed idea, but is quite sure everything will change, and much faster than you think; if you do not natively understand this stuff, the transition will be hard.

28:51 Trust makes money land six weeks faster
Gagan says he volunteers in local politics in his spare time, and the biggest takeaway is understanding how valuable trust is. He gives a concrete comparison: in a nonprofit, after a donor verbally commits $50,000 to you, the probability that the money actually lands in your account is only about 20% to 50%; in Silicon Valley, that probability is about 75% to 100%. The difference is that if you are certain the money is coming, you can confidently move forward, and by the time the check actually arrives you have already advanced six weeks, which makes the check more valuable still. Conversely, without trust you change your approach out of fear the donor will be unhappy, drift from your mission, and are left with only anxiety and stress. He thinks this can be transplanted into schools: trust students to do what they want to do.

32:01 With no grades there is no fulcrum to push against
Asked how to handle disruptive students — like Zuckerberg, who nearly got expelled for FaceMash — Gagan says there must of course be red lines, rules for things like sexual harassment and publicly humiliating others, and you need to build trust and a positive-sum atmosphere. But he says one core principle of the academy sidesteps the problem entirely: with no grades and no exams, the resistance students have to push against is already far smaller. So if you want to build FaceMash, go build it, and he is willing to defend that right even if he personally finds the idea weird and does not like it. He thinks that as long as you create an environment of trust and keep students from developing an anti-authority mindset, you unlock a huge amount of creativity and opportunity. Amjad adds that this drive to test boundaries can be channeled in healthy directions: kids who learn to program and hack on Roblox, rather than being sent to prison, could be put in a sandbox, have their talent discovered, and be steered into cybersecurity jobs or even government.

item.title: Jensen Huang: Saying There's a 10% Chance AI Destroys Humanity Is Irresponsible
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-ezra-黄仁勋-说-ai-有-10-概率毁灭人类是不负责任的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-ezra-黄仁勋-说-ai-有-10-概率毁灭人类是不负责任的/
item.description: He concedes AI will change every job, but treats the risk of losing control as a solvable engineering problem: if a lab truly believed it had lost control, the right answer is not to ship the product, not to buy the most compute while asking to be slowed down.
item.content:encoded:
He concedes AI will change every job, but treats the risk of losing control as a solvable engineering problem: if a lab truly believed it had lost control, the right answer is not to ship the product, not to buy the most compute while asking to be slowed down.

Huang rarely engages the AI doomer argument head-on; here he gives concrete positions on alignment, evaluation and the compute split, and concedes the cycle will eventually turn. The unit economics in the back half are worth more than the front half.

6:28 Reading scans got automated, and there are more radiologists
Huang uses radiology as his core case: over the past decade computer vision reached superhuman levels, AI has permeated every radiology application, and it can detect any abnormality and any disease. But reading scans is a task a radiologist does, not the purpose of the job — the purpose is to diagnose disease and help patients. Once reading is automated, doctors can handle more cases, hospital revenue rises, and more radiologists are needed. From this he draws the distinction between the purpose of a job and the tasks of a job.

9:32 For jobs like customer service, the task is the job
Huang concedes AI will change every job and automate a great many tasks, and he explicitly names a category of job that gets replaced wholesale: when the job and the task are one and the same, as with phone customer service, the job itself is that task. But he offers counter-evidence too: AI only became genuinely useful in the past six months, after 15 years of getting it to run at all, and in those six months $500 billion of venture capital went into AI-native companies.

22:01 Data on 26,000 Chinese students: homework faster, exams down
Ezra cites a study from China: 26,000 students in grades 7 through 12, with staggered AI adoption. The result was an 18% rise in homework scores and a 30% drop in completion time, but a 20% decline in monthly exam scores within six months and an 18% to 24% decline on high-stakes entrance exams, with the full penalty showing up only about two years later. Huang's response: he agrees completely with that last part, just as nobody does long division anymore and the multiplication table is being forgotten, but he doesn't think it matters — ‘we'll discover new skills, they just may not be those.’

35:28 Cheating isn't malice, it's the cheapest path in compute
Huang unpacks the Hugging Face agent attack: software given an objective function optimizes toward the objective, that's just what the algorithm does. If you tell software to score perfectly on this test, the most obvious move is to go find the answers; if it can't do that at all, the second most obvious move is to figure out who the smartest kid in class is and copy off him. Only the third approach is to decompose the problem, go learn the material, and grind it out — that consumes the most compute and the most energy, so unless you align it and tell it that's how it must solve the problem, the software takes the most obvious path.

40:48 A company with agency can't say it needs to be saved
Ezra relays the labs' public position: they face a hybrid problem of engineering, alignment and operational excellence, and competition with each other and with China is pushing them too fast, so they feel they are losing control of what they're building and want outside help to slow down. Huang rejects the frame: these are companies with agency, CEOs with agency, and they're using that agency to say ‘we need help.’ His analogy: if a car company believed it was about to ship an unsafe product, it has the ability, the power and the responsibility not to ship it — and it already has the incentive not to.

59:49 Hinton's prediction has no scientific basis
Ezra mentions that Jeffrey Hinton said a 10% chance of societal destruction is not unreasonable; Huang answers directly: I would tell Jeff that saying that is irresponsible, that his predictions have consistently been wrong, that the 10% figure is not grounded in science or in research — ‘just because it comes from a scientist doesn't make it science.’ He then brings up the old score: the advice that nobody should go into radiology, the claim that deep learning would surpass radiologists within five years, which didn't happen; and if that scares young people out of college because they think they won't find work, that's harmful.

1:17:30 The R&D split has to flip from 80/20
Huang gives a concrete split: at NVIDIA roughly 10% to 20% of people do design and 80% do verification, whereas most labs today, understandably, put 80% into capability and 20% into safety, verification and evaluation. He says that ratio will flip, and that's the transition he means. He asks labs not to ship him anything unevaluated: don't send NVIDIA any product that hasn't been evaluated with a human in the loop. His position is that safety, alignment, evaluation, guardrails, sandboxes, containment, monitoring, telemetry and external AI monitoring are all AI technologies and should be accelerated to the maximum.

1:24:48 The math on a one-gigawatt AI factory
Huang gives the unit economics of the new computing era: building a one-gigawatt data center, a one-gigawatt AI factory, costs $50 billion, and it can be rented out for $40 to $50 billion a year. He describes the shift from retrieval based computing (retrieving files, hence data center) to generative computing, with compute per user rising sharply; add agents also using generative AI, and it isn't just a billion people using computers but hundreds of billions of agents plus people, which could mean a billionfold rise in compute required.

item.title: The UK's productivity crisis was a statistical error: 0.7% became 1.3%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-moreorless-英国生产率危机是统计错误-0-7-被改成-1-3/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-moreorless-英国生产率危机是统计错误-0-7-被改成-1-3/
item.description: Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst performer on productivity among developed economies may have been an ONS miscalculation of hours worked — counting people on holiday as working 40 hours inflated the denominator and pushed productivity down.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst performer on productivity among developed economies may have been an ONS miscalculation of hours worked — counting people on holiday as working 40 hours inflated the denominator and pushed productivity down.

Medium information density, but the UK productivity revision alone is enough to change your read on the "British disease"; the other three segments are routine fact-checks you can take or leave.

1:05 The UK productivity crisis was a calculation
After the financial crisis, UK productivity growth was estimated at 0.7% a year, the worst among developed economies, and it became the raw material for fifteen years of the "productivity puzzle." After the ONS changed how it measures hours worked, that number became 1.3%, nearly double. Output and GDP did not change; only the denominator did: Britons actually work far fewer hours than previously thought. Chris Giles says pre-crisis growth was 2%, and 2% means productivity doubles roughly every 35 years, while 0.7% means it takes a century to double; 1.3% falls in between. Britain is no longer an international outlier, but growth is still below the pre-crisis rate.

4:16 Asking people their weekly hours cannot be trusted
The old method simply asked respondents how many hours they worked in a week and took the answer at face value. The problem came at follow-up: if no one answered the door in August, the ONS carried over the 40 hours that person had reported three months earlier, plugging in a 40 — when that person was very likely on holiday and had not worked a single hour. The OECD recommended back in 2018 that countries stop doing this; the UK took eight years to change. Giles says that over those eight years people wrote a batch of "UK productivity crisis" articles that no longer hold up. He admits it is infuriating, but the change is in the right direction.

11:38 One in ten Irish people as clergy is a misquote
The book said that in the 1960s one in every ten Irish children became a nun, priest or Christian Brother. The 1961 census shows 18,854 Catholic clergy and nuns, 2,125 Christian Brothers and other religious brothers, and 4,842 seminarians, for a total of 25,821 — 1/104 of the population. The 1951 ratio was 1/127. The original source is research by Mary Daly, who looked only at students sitting the 1966 leaving certificate exam, when fewer than 20% of the school-age population took that exam, about 12,000 people, of whom roughly one in ten entered religious life. That qualifier was lost in retelling and became "all children." The author has said subsequent editions will be corrected.

14:41 Grid queue numbers are inflated by applications
Between November 2024 and June 2025, cumulative electricity demand in the UK grid connection queue jumped from about 41 GW to 125 GW, tripling in six months, with data centres accounting for 73 GW. But queuing is cheap, like booking a table at a popular restaurant months ahead, and many projects will never actually be built or will shrink. Ofgem estimates that if all this data centre demand materialised, the cost would be close to £700 billion, nearly a quarter of UK annual GDP. A 2025 government report projected 6 GW would be needed by 2030, while another queue analysis reckons about 20 GW has serious financial backing behind it. Johnny Gowdy of Regen says no one knows how much will ultimately be built.

17:45 The data centre emissions comparison counts only direct emissions
Foxglove's analysis claims two planned data centres at full load would emit more carbon than ExxonMobil's UK operations. That comparison counts only ExxonMobil's own operational emissions, excluding the petrol and diesel it sells — which is the main source of emissions, something an ordinary reader may not spot. Foxglove also assumes the data centres run at 100% power year-round, while a scholar studying AI's carbon footprint uses 65%. More important is the power source: the planning documents for these two projects say that initially, because they cannot connect to the grid, they will use on-site gas generation. The UK grid as a whole is about half renewable and only 30% gas, so this batch of data centres amounts to stimulating demand for higher-carbon generation.

23:00 Vinyl's physical limits mattered less, not more
The 1950s story goes: the closer a record gets to the centre, the lower the linear speed, and the less bass and brightness a groove can hold, so you put the quiet song at the end of a side. Mitchell Sterling's database has 2,284 albums and 27,000 songs spanning 1953 to the present. Measured by relative loudness, before 1982 closing tracks averaged about 0.65 dB quieter than earlier tracks; after 1982, when cassette sales overtook vinyl in the US and the constraint disappeared, the gap widened to about 1.5 dB. In the streaming era after 2010, the gap is still twice what it was in the vinyl era. In other words, the less the physical limit mattered, the quieter closing tracks became.

26:02 The quiet ending went from constraint to artistic device
Sterling defines a quiet, acoustic closing track as the "typical quiet acoustic farewell." In the 1950s more than 60% of albums ended with a quiet, acoustic song; as recordings overall got louder, that absolute share slid all the way down to under one-sixth in the 1980s; by the 2000s and 2020s it had recovered to about one-third. Sterling's analogy is the save icon on a floppy disk: the constraint is long gone, the habit remains. He also found in streaming data that an album's last track averages longer, more acoustic and sadder — but that is an average, and hip-hop, heavy metal and electronic music are full of loud exceptions.

item.title: Why used cars are selling for new-car prices
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-indicator-二手车为什么卖出了新车的价格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-indicator-二手车为什么卖出了新车的价格/
item.description: New-car price increases drag used cars up with them through the ‘price waterfall’; pandemic production cuts left the car market digesting the shock for years, like a snake swallowing a mouse; and US automakers simply stopped building cheap sedans — the cars you can get for $10,000 to $15,000 went from 5 years old to 9 years old.
item.content:encoded:
New-car price increases drag used cars up with them through the ‘price waterfall’; pandemic production cuts left the car market digesting the shock for years, like a snake swallowing a mouse; and US automakers simply stopped building cheap sedans — the cars you can get for $10,000 to $15,000 went from 5 years old to 9 years old.

One episode that lays out all three mechanisms behind expensive used cars, plus a counterintuitive place to look for a deal: used EVs. Medium information density, but the conclusions are directly usable.

3:08 New-car price increases have actually leveled off
A lot of people assume the car market is still in runaway inflation, but the data doesn't say that. From 2019 to now, new-car prices rose 4.3% annualized, while overall CPI rose slightly under 4% annualized over the same period — not a wild gap. In other words, the new-car line has basically returned to the broader market's level. The real problem is the other half of the market: over the same period, used-car prices rose about 5.5% annualized, beating both inflation and new cars. Today a used car just three years old averages over $32,000. So ‘cars are expensive’ is mainly not a new-car problem — it's a used-car problem.

4:13 Used-car prices follow new cars, and tariffs feed through too
The first mechanism is called the ‘price waterfall’: used-car prices follow new-car prices, and for the same brand and model, when the new-car price goes up or down, the used one moves with it. This isn't new. The key point is that even if a used car was built before a tariff took effect, its price is still affected by the tariff — because the tariff raises the cost of new cars and of the materials that go into them, the whole water level of the waterfall rises, and the used cars downstream get lifted along with it. So hoping that ‘I'm buying an old car, the tariff has nothing to do with me’ doesn't hold up.

5:17 Pandemic production cuts are a snake swallowing a mouse, not yet digested
The second mechanism is supply. The drop in car production in 2020 means that years later — say, in 2026 — used-car buyers have fewer cars to choose from. Jeremy Robb's metaphor is ‘watching a snake swallow a mouse’: the low-production bottleneck propagates down the timeline, and when supply is thin, prices are generally high. The car market is that snake still slowly digesting the used-car mouse, and its stomach is still unhappy. This mechanism explains why, long after the pandemic, the selection of used cars is still narrow.

5:17 Automakers deliberately killed off cheap sedans
The third mechanism is a business decision, not an act of God. Ivan Drury says the automakers' judgment was ‘nobody wants sedans, so let's build more big SUVs’ — big SUVs selling for $60,000, $70,000, $80,000, even $100,000, while the $20,000-to-$30,000 entry-level sedan was removed from the market entirely. US automakers have all but emptied out the whole category; Ford stopped building ordinary sedans like the Fiesta years ago; the Japanese and Korean brands still have a few, the German brands fewer. The result is that an entire vehicle category has been compressed into a handful of choices, and anyone who wants ‘just a tool to get from A to B’ has to wait in line.

6:18 A $10,000-to-$15,000 car is now four years older
Stack those three mechanisms together and the cheapest segment of the market has essentially been ‘scrapped’. Ivan Drury looked into this range: in 2019, $10,000 to $15,000 bought you a car about 5 years old; today, the same money buys a car approaching 9 years old with roughly 100,000 miles on it. This isn't just a change in numbers — it creates a personal-finance trap: trying to stay on budget brings on more expenses instead. A 100,000-mile car usually needs more repairs, and the expensive, annoying parts — water pumps, timing belts — will fail, and anyone who can't do the work has to pay someone else to fix it. The money you saved on the purchase price may flow right back out through the repair bill.

7:22 Auto loan rates have doubled, but inflation data doesn't count them
There's another big cost that the statistical definitions miss: interest. In 2019, a borrower with ‘good but not great’ credit could get a 4.5% auto loan rate; today the same person with the same loan gets close to 9%, roughly double. The key point is that the agencies that record inflation data only count the price of the car, not the monthly interest expense. So the official numbers don't look that bad, but the actual monthly payment burden on car buyers is much heavier. Ivan's advice is that you have to run the numbers yourself now: if you can get a very low APR on a new car, that low rate can completely erase the premise that ‘buying used is the better deal’.

8:27 Used EVs are the one corner still on sale
The car market isn't one single thing. Ivan Drury says there's one segment where you can still find a bargain: EVs. He describes EV resale value as ‘atrocious’, because of misconceptions about EVs — how long the battery lasts, how reliable they are. Those misconceptions push used EV prices down, which in turn creates an opportunity for buyers, and he is bullish on this market. He admits the technology really is iterating fast, which makes people feel that ‘buy today and it's obsolete tomorrow’, but for a lot of cars, even once the tech is outdated, it still works fine.

item.title: US Debt Tops $40 Trillion: Even the Doves Are Calling Themselves Hawks Now
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-planetmoney-美国债务破-40-万亿-连鸽派都改口当鹰派了/
