item.description: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weak link in the barrel isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
item.content:encoded:
AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weak link in the barrel isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.

A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.

16:07 Individual productivity tripled, delivery only sped up three days
NetEase ran the numbers last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design doc to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the whole process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves shot up fast, but some staves aren't people — they're process — and they didn't improve at all. So AI adoption has to clear three hurdles: cognition, landing on individual short-range tasks, and transforming process and organization. The third is the hardest.

20:11 Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. It used to be 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself isn't done well, because no one listens attentively the whole time and may miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people can leave comments and follow-up questions; an AI agent produces a preliminary list of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirm and supplement; problem-solving and decision-making become dedicated meetings.

28:20 SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may really die, while truly good SaaS that has already entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past, humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, a large number of agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, audit APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volume will far exceed the number and actions of humans, it will grow enormously, and the more it's called the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that this Service is critical enough inside the company.

32:21 Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong and what if they leave. There used to be no solution, but now you can distill or extract the actions, scripts, and behaviors of good salespeople into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training needs to distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data the salesperson has had, from calls, WeChat, email, etc., and have AI simulate various customers to train the salesperson. Online sales is purely digital and on record; for offline sales, recommend or even require a recording card — after a visit, record a two-to-three-minute voice memo while memory is fresh, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them), but they don't mind a recording card, because it's also useful for their own customer review.

44:31 Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead agent legions back to the front line
Ruan Liang judges that middle management will become fewer and fewer, but not necessarily eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer and fewer, while elite individuals with strong skills will become more and more. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously, socialized division of labor split software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future, organizations will look more and more like a distributed structure, with countless highly capable engineers, a mother peak commanding some engineers, and countless agents fighting a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation scenario: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company has to pay might be some kind of OPC.

50:35 AI value formula: quality times time saved
Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI value = quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight points, AI also makes it at eight points, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time, and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Claude, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheaper ones can too.

59:40 Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era, they found a group of people whose token consumption was astonishing, and whose work output and work value were also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about AI abuse causing waste; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, there are fewer layers, and the chain is shorter.

1:11:50 The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision processes and decision rationales. This year NetEase preserved historical decisions, incorporated them into the knowledge base, combined the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed back the original hundreds of cases for the agent to judge, achieving over 90% accuracy. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts agents they built themselves, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a human adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment actions enter the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, essentially human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

item.title: Mooncakes sell for only two months a year, yet they've become a 28.2 billion yuan business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.description: Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from the gifting occasion and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from the gifting occasion and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.

Worth listening to for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand the holiday consumption business, but information density is low, with much of the runtime spent on explaining regional styles and flavors, and the business mechanics concentrated in the middle-to-late sections.

6:06 Zongzi can sell year-round, mooncakes cannot
Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all year round, and Wufangzhai (五芳斋) even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday settings. Mooncakes' problem is not that the craft can't achieve long shelf life, but that it is defined as a ‘traditional festival pastry mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival’, and the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from its festival through shelf life and channels, while mooncakes cannot.

12:12 The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
Lotus seed paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use the five kernels: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of this line is to push up ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, green and red shreds, and inferior nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the order of the ingredient list is enough to judge how much of what is actually in there.

26:30 Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess but because of structure. Outside is flaky pastry, in the middle is a custard layer, and at the very center is the lava layer, with the custard layer acting as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point must be designed — solid during transport, turning to flowing liquid only after a few seconds in the microwave. If heated too much, the lava is absorbed dry by the pastry and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

37:34 ‘Everything can be a mooncake’ has five preconditions
Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot and sour soup mooncakes can't be made because there's too much water to contain; second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also loved by microbes, so processing temperature and sterilization processes must be tested repeatedly; third is particle size — too large and the pastry can't hold it, too fine and you can't taste it; fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply disappear once baked; fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are ones confirmed by generation after generation.

44:40 Choosing an OEM is not a matter of bigger is better
When big brands make branded mooncakes through OEMs, there's a common misconception: you must choose the best OEM in the country. But the top OEMs' production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days of safe production. Also, the nine major regional styles correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant (广州酒家) to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they don't have that capability or production line.

48:44 Flexible lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — wrapping and forming machines can do their part, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes too. If a company has only 50 employees, it can directly use the factory's existing mooncakes and only needs to design the gift box. This small-batch, fast-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can be a corporate customization business.

51:47 The 28.2 billion yuan scale is propped up by gifting
In 2025 China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons and sales scale was 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces, at 100 grams about 5.18 billion pieces, and across a population of 1.4 billion that's an average of three to four per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales scale is about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. That mooncakes can do 28.2 billion selling only two months a year comes down to the gifting attribute — brands prepare large amounts of PR gifts at the two nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

58:55 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
In 2022 the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement placing boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit under key supervision. So the highest mooncake price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it cannot exceed 500 yuan. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor inside, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

item.title: AI for Science Is Stuck on the Last 0.001 Points, Not on Compute
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.description: ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap in the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to judge ‘you got this paper wrong’.
item.content:encoded:
ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap in the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to judge ‘you got this paper wrong’.

High information density, but it takes some patience: the first half covers ERA's mechanics, the second half covers contrails, wildfires and quantum computing, all first-hand detail.

9:24 ERA takes chat as input and returns a scored notebook
ERA's product form isn't having people write config files — you just start chatting. Because mapping a scientific problem onto a scorable task is itself non-obvious, Michael Brenner wrote a dedicated agent to conversationally help you define which score to optimize. Once the conversation ends, it generates a Python notebook underneath containing a function that produces a score, and then the system starts mutating that notebook in a ‘clever way’, continually proposing new code to push the score higher.

10:24 It doesn't always pick the best candidate
ERA runs Monte Carlo Tree Search internally, keeping hundreds or thousands of notebook candidates at once in a tree-shaped pool. Selection uses the upper confidence bound from reinforcement learning: estimate the 95th percentile outcome of a mutation and pick the one with the highest optimistic upper bound. So it doesn't always greedily pick the currently best-performing notebook; sometimes it picks the fifth best, in order to explore more efficiently. It has also tried combining the ideas of two candidates to generate a third.

18:38 Evolutionary coding was stuck for decades because random mutation is useless
Platt says people have been doing evolutionary coding since the 1970s — mutating Lisp code and the like — but it never took off, because random mutation in code space is basically worthless: just like DNA, the vast majority of mutations are harmful. ERA works because the inner loop is itself an AI that knows which direction to try, which amounts to having a meaningful gradient underneath. The price is that it also overfits, and it also goes off the rails in ‘genie wish’ fashion.

22:44 Predictive models and descriptive models are two different things
John Platt splits scientific modeling into two kinds: a predictive model only seeks the lowest error rate on some dataset; a descriptive model is what science actually wants — it contains some internal description of reality, so it can extrapolate. His example is Newton: an apple falling can be fitted, but gravity isn't about apples, and if you take a model that only fits apples and ask it about planets, it has no planetary data and knows nothing. He admits the line is blurry, because the scientist themself also constrains the model with a pile of known facts and intuitions.

31:59 This is a power tool, and it will cut your fingers off
Faced with multiple hypothesis testing and overfitting, Platt's answer isn't a new method but a harsher old one: because ERA is a power tool, you have to be stricter than before, with a holdout buried so deep you never look at it yourself. He states plainly that no system yet discovers entirely new physics or entirely new science, and scientists are still responsible for judging whether a conclusion is descriptive.

39:18 AI is stuck on the last 0.001 points
Ira pushed the score very close, but it didn't close the gap in roughly the last 30 places, because nobody goes and scrapes off that last 0.001 points. This exposes the system's real structure: the inner layer is a machine running for hours to produce candidates, and the outer layer is a human making judgments like ‘you got this paper wrong’. Platt compares it to a graduate student who never sleeps and is extremely eager — you tell it a direction, it goes and tries, but when it gets stuck a human has to change the approach.

48:08 The counterfactual model stalled the team for two years
To judge which contrail to avoid, you need to know how much warming it actually causes, and that's a counterfactual problem: you can't enter the universe where the contrail doesn't exist. The team produced a counterfactual model that worked for outgoing longwave radiation, but they could never build one for the part that reflects sunlight, and it stalled them for two years. They even self-tested with a dataset where contrails were artificially injected, and their own attempt couldn't pass their own test. In the end ERA found a simple model that searches over all confounders, passed the test, and cracked the problem.

1:24:27 A wildfire is best put out before it's room-sized
Google has a crisis resilience effort, and one project in it is called Firesat: a wildfire is extremely easy to extinguish when it's only as big as ‘this room’, and once it reaches an acre it's far harder, while the growth from room-sized to an acre may be exponential. The plan is a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation using mid-wave IR (which corresponds to blackbody radiation, exactly the temperature of fire) for detection; about 50 to 80 satellites could cover the globe, spot a fire about 5 meters across, and raise an alarm within 15 to 20 minutes. The partner is the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, the satellites are built by Muon Space, and one prototype has already launched.

item.title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.description: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.

The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser with information and worth hearing.

6:06 This visit has no substantive agenda at all
Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has "there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all." Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pageantry and the cameras, and incidentally to push something like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, this actually makes them less nervous — because a more confrontational meeting is what would make them anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized that; and Beijing, watching the chaos in Washington, sees the American president himself often in a position they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed badly, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether things slip into the scenario they are trying hardest to avoid.

9:25 Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
Gewirtz characterizes this visit as "we are in a space of symbolism and optics." He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pageantry and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and American interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy, and that handshake photo, and got a step back from the other side on third-world countries or nuclear issues. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration does not even seem to have attempted to design a set of "deliverables." Gewirtz says "it doesn't even seem like they're trying." So what to watch is not where things go wrong, but "where is the trade happening."

11:37 The direction of concessions has been flipped entirely
Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China have been flipped into "gifts" from China to the US. Pageantry and cameras are what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used not to sell these things, so opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now, if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it matters is not to score the administration but because it reflects what happens when the power gap in superpower competition narrows — very small differences, interpersonal dynamics, can produce much larger displacements in the overall strategic picture.

12:39 US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
Gewirtz uses the "K-shaped" idea for US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel — dense exchanges of visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the competitive reality and the actions parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses the metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying "truce" or "detente" sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic and quite unstable, moving in both directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether that holds as the K widens.

22:03 The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election and became the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or transform it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on "a new cold war in an age of doubt" — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about does not exist, then this is a moment of "incredible fluidity." He says he has no confidence in the direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy in the medium term, and Beijing has no confidence either.

31:24 Chinese officials cannot talk about risks they have no solution for
Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that is correct. But he says: heads of American AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for, and they all do; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying "we, the Communist Party, see it, we will handle it, we have a solution." So the real question is: should we treat what we can see from Beijing as everything, or acknowledge there is more in the system that we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — Americans then predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said that was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing did nail the Jell-O to the wall: the Great Firewall.

35:37 Beijing has not decided how to regulate open models
Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing still has not given the single most important thing: how it plans to regulate open weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this "the trillion dollar question." Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision has not been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself has not decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts the Trump administration: it did not make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

41:55 What to prepare for is not China's decline but Xi's decline
Gewirtz says that a few years ago the "peak China" debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least for the moment on a relatively sustainable path. But he thinks the real question is not that, but "do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline" — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By "prepare" he does not mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses the change could absolutely be worse for the US — "That doesn't mean he's going to mellow."

item.title: Canada Wants Into the EU: This Is a Permanent Break With America, Not a Wait for Trump to Leave
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.description: Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's rate.
item.content:encoded:
Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's rate.

Medium information density, but the nonexistent "associate member" status, Carney's European network and book club, and the EU's Brexit-driven red line are three judgments you won't hear anywhere else.

0:00 Canada wants to be the EU's first associate member, but the status doesn't exist
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Canada is negotiating to become an associate member of the EU. But the show says it plainly: the EU has no such thing as "associate member" — you're either a member, paying into the budget, accepting free movement of people and seamless truck crossings, or you're not. All 27 current members are in Europe, sharing borders, regulations, and mostly the euro. So what Canada gets will be a status invented for it, with details still under negotiation. What Carney wants isn't another buyer but a group of "like-minded" countries to build, together, the institutions and technological capabilities that America's "wrecking ball" can't reach.

3:01 Canada once saw itself as Europeans living in North America
This isn't a new idea; it's a return to an old identity. In the first half of the 20th century, some Canadians genuinely saw themselves as "Europeans living in North America" — today's oldest Canadians were born British subjects, and Canada didn't open an embassy in Washington until the 1920s. On the eve of World War II, Canada's trade with Britain still exceeded its trade with the US. After the war America became the center of gravity of the West, the auto industry integrated in the 1960s, NAFTA took effect in 1994, and Canadian elites switched from Oxford and Cambridge to Harvard and Yale. Trump's tensions reopened a forgotten historical question: where do Canadians belong in the world?

6:13 The 51st state isn't a trade negotiation, it's a sovereignty question
When Trump returned for a second term, he didn't just want to renegotiate a trade deal; he questioned the territorial integrity of allies like Canada and Denmark, and said openly he wanted Canada to become the 51st state. The show's judgment: if it were only a trade renegotiation, you could negotiate; once sovereignty is touched, you're touching something highly emotional, sensitive, electorally meaningful and bound up with a country's self-image. One Canadian official, after reading every Trump biography he could find, concluded that the 51st state talk was "price discovery" — throwing out an outrageous idea to test the reaction. Whatever the intent, the effect was real: Carney went from 25 points behind in the polls to winning overnight.

8:17 Carney defined the trade war as "we are being attacked"
Carney had two signature moments after taking office. One was the Davos speech, landing right in the middle of the Greenland crisis, with Trump scheduled to speak the next day; Carney went first and delivered the clearest anti-Trumpist manifesto yet: Canadians' old comfortable assumption that geography and alliances automatically deliver prosperity and security no longer holds. The second came when the US imposed tariffs: instead of backing down he escalated, hitting back with tariffs of his own, and he still wouldn't budge after the final round of trade talks collapsed. Asked at a press conference why it felt like war was about to start that day, his answer was "because we are being attacked." The show notes that for a technocrat and centrist to escalate is counterintuitive, and that is precisely what has made him a leader of the Western allies' anti-Trump movement — for better or worse.

11:22 Carney's European network matters more than his policies
A North American prime minister with an unusually large number of European friends: an Oxford economics doctorate, the first foreigner to run the Bank of England. Macron was a banker, German Chancellor Merz worked at BlackRock, Finnish President Stubb also came from finance — Carney knows them all. In Ottawa he also has a book club whose members are political heavyweights and industry leaders, with a Fight Club-style rule: "the first rule of book club is you don't talk about book club." Most of them were educated at Oxford or Cambridge, are familiar with Europe, and remain in touch with the prime minister, feeding him exactly the kinds of ideas about how to bring Canada closer to Europe. The show says interviewees were far more secretive about the book club than about Canada's plan to join the EU.

14:27 The talks aren't just trade — they're data cables and Erasmus
What the two sides are discussing goes far beyond tariffs: laying data cables connecting Europe and Canada; jointly building data centers, cloud storage and satellite networks placed beyond the reach of American tech giants; building new pipelines in Canada to send natural gas to the East Coast and on to Europe; using icebreakers to open Arctic shipping routes for fertilizer. They also plan to entwine Canadian and EU research institutions to create a network of academic and scientific output that can rival the American system. Canada is even pushing to join the EU's Erasmus student exchange program — the show says this is a big deal in Europe and has led to a lot of marriages. If a generation of Canadians goes to school in Paris, Spain and Italy, and a generation of Italians comes to Ottawa, Montreal and Vancouver, then what's being negotiated isn't just economics but social ties deeper than the flow of natural gas and minerals.

17:45 The EU's red line: no one can think you can quit and still get the perks
For Europe, Canada is a "shiny new toy": it has raw materials, critical minerals and energy Europe has long coveted, its values are similar, and Carney speaking French and English and making his first trip to Paris and London rather than Washington means a lot to Europeans. But the risks are just as clear. The EU is haunted by Brexit, and its long-standing red line is that "no one can ever be allowed to think they can leave the club and keep enjoying the benefits" — if major countries start quitting and demanding a Canada-style deal, that would be fatal to the EU. So the puzzle Carney has to solve is: get Canada a large share of trade and connectivity benefits without creating a precedent that lets a country like Italy say "we don't like these regulations, let's quit and become a Canada-style member — no rules but all the benefits."

19:54 The real pain hasn't arrived yet, and the White House is betting geography decides fate
There are concerns inside Canada: how much sovereignty would an associate membership with a fuzzy identity require giving up, which regulations would it accept, what happens to immigration — conservative voters and mainstream newspaper columnists are all asking. But the bigger fear is the cost of decoupling from the US, because so far it's only a war of words and the real pain hasn't hit the Canadian economy yet: two-thirds of exports depend on the US, and that's a lot of people's businesses and jobs. The White House's judgment is that geography is destiny, Canada is right there, decades of economic ties are real, and in the end Canada will be pulled back to the negotiating table — flirting with Europe won't change economic reality. You can't force Canadian businesses to do business in Europe when a few miles (or, in Canada, a few kilometers) across the border sits an attractive market.

item.title: Ranking Psychology's Classic Experiments: Many Conclusions Don't Survive Replication
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.description: The Milgram shock experiment still replicates, which is itself absurd; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.
item.content:encoded:
The Milgram shock experiment still replicates, which is itself absurd; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.

Two philosophers plus a psychologist rank classic studies from D to S, and along the way settle accounts with the replication crisis, Zimbardo's fraudulent original notes, and small samples.

10:08 Milgram still replicating is itself absurd
Milgram recruited New Haven workers in a Yale basement, got them to believe they were shocking another person, with the voltage labeled up to 300 volts and marked dangerous; the person being "shocked" was actually a trained actor, and about 65% of them pressed all the way to the end. He ran a large number of variants, manipulating whether the experimenter wore a white coat, the distance to the person being shocked, and which university's name was on the door. The study directly rewrote psychology's ethics review system; today this kind of experiment can't be done. Dave says that a social psychology study from the 50s and 60s that still replicates is itself "[ __ ] banana," which is why it goes in the S tier — he's using replication as the bar, not fame.

29:20 The Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 people
Darley and Batson had seminary students go to the other side of campus to speak on the parable of the Good Samaritan, and arranged for a visibly injured, groaning person asking for help along the way; the manipulated variable was the time pressure they were under. It turned out time pressure predicted whether they stopped to help better than what topic they were going to speak on. But Dave points out that the whole experiment had only 40 subjects total, and after splitting into groups the samples were tiny. He groups this kind of study with the telephone-booth coin experiment as a common disease of 60s and 70s social psychology: severely underpowered, "even if they got it right, they got it right by accident." Paul says it's great as material for making people reflect on human nature, but as a scientific finding he doesn't trust it, and gives it a D.

48:38 On the cloth mother, mothers already knew
Harlow separated infant monkeys from their mothers and built two surrogate mothers: a wire frame with a bottle attached, and a soft, huggable cloth one that provided no milk. Except when they had to nurse, the infants stayed on the cloth mother the rest of the time. This refuted the behaviorist explanation that "infants love their mothers because the mother provides food," and supported the role of contact comfort. The episode clarifies that Harlow did not actually shock the monkeys; what's hard to watch is the footage of frightened infants rushing to the cloth mother and clinging on for dear life. He also called the isolation apparatus the "pit of despair" and the restraint device the "rape rack" in published articles, and the reaction on the show was "he's just a psychopath." Tamler argues for the lowest score, not because of cruelty, but because these studies didn't show anything any mother would know by intuition the moment you asked her.

1:10:52 The prison experiment's author was coaching guards to abuse
The original notes and recordings dug up on the Stanford prison experiment show that Zimbardo himself was coaching the people randomly assigned to be guards to engage in abusive behavior. If the intended story of the study is "put people in this role and they spontaneously become sadists," then on the available evidence that conclusion is highly suspect — he didn't report how much he pushed them. David thinks this is close to scientific fraud, groups it with "the dog torturer," and no longer teaches it. But David also cautions: across the Milgram and Asch series, people differ, and some said "screw you, I'm not doing it" at the lowest shock level. Tamler adds that when he interviewed Zimbardo, the latter talked about Milgram, saying Milgram did no psychological screening and some of the people who showed up might have been sociopaths, while Zimbardo claimed he did screen, using that to prove these were normal people.

1:15:59 Even adults fail the false belief task
The false belief task comes from Premack and Woodruff's paper "Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind"; Dennett proposed this design in his commentary: Sally puts a toy in a box and leaves, Anne moves it to a basket, and you ask where Sally will look for it when she returns. Children before age three or four say the place where the toy actually is, and around age five they start getting it right; this shift from failure to success is one of the most robust findings in all of developmental psychology. But Paul and Susan Birch tested adults and found adults find it hard too — there's an immediate intuition pointing to "where the thing actually is" that has to be inhibited; he demonstrates it live in his intro course, and about a third of the students get it wrong. What bothers Tamler is that once the paradigm got hot, the whole field shifted from that interesting question to the methodology itself, and the test became the construct.

1:24:06 To deny the methods are all broken, you must accept ESP
Daryl Bem published a paper in a top social psychology journal in 2011 claiming to have found precognition: subjects first rated their preference for unfamiliar Chinese characters, and only afterward were shown emotional images as primes; the characters that were positively primed afterward had been rated higher beforehand. He made all his materials and data public, and Paul thinks he genuinely believed the result. Bem's defense is a dilemma: if you say my research isn't good research, then almost all research in social psychology isn't good research — so either admit your methods are reliable and accept ESP, or admit the methods are unreliable. Paul says he was furious at the time: this would overturn our entire understanding of space and time, and you want to accept it on a p less than 0.05. This is also the driving force behind the Bayesian countermovement in psychology: results should be compared against prior plausibility, not against 0.05.

1:29:09 Delayed gratification may measure trust, not self-control
Mischel and Ebbesen had preschoolers choose between taking a small reward immediately and waiting for two. What's more interesting in the original study is that some children spontaneously used strategies — thinking of the marshmallow as a white cloud, singing, distracting themselves; Tamler says they were "tying themselves to the mast." The problem comes later: following these children and claiming the wait time predicts SAT scores, and Tamler just read that the SAT correlation used only 35 children, yet schools started teaching delayed gratification on that basis. He dismantles the premises that "delayed gratification causes success" would need: it has to be teachable, rather than merely capturing some natural difference that already predicts on its own; self-control has to be the active ingredient, rather than the willingness to please the teacher; and there's the question of why the child believes the other person will really give another one — if you're in an impoverished environment, why wait.

1:32:12 Social priming collapsed, and conceptual priming was buried with it
Bargh's classic study: subjects were randomly assigned a set of words to unscramble, and if those words were related to concepts like elderly and retirement, the speed at which they walked from room A to room B after the task was measured, and it turned out those primed with the elderly concept walked more slowly. It claims that stimuli entirely outside consciousness can influence behavior — you don't even know you were assigned elderly words. Tamler recalls that when he had just finished his degree, this kind of research was at its peak. Paul says social priming has since been shown to be wrong, but what really bothers him is the consequence: its collapse took down with it conceptual priming (for example, flashing "doctor" to prime "nurse") and other very robust, easily replicated findings — that's what the architecture of the mind actually looks like; the problem was extrapolating it directly to effect sizes in behavior and everyday life.

item.title: No Winners in a Pig-Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Too
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.description: In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.

The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI-enabled fraud at high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwarfare, which is loosely connected to the theme and can be skipped as needed.

4:11 AI makes scam emails free to mass-produce
Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an invitation to be on the program in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; when he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," the model immediately produced a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — not that scammers have become better writers, but that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammatical errors and polished phrasing, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

7:14 Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime ever
Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who keep a share of what they steal, and the enslaved, coerced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do what is called pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened before slaughter. The con often runs from weeks to more than a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependency first, and only at the end introduces an "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars from victims every year.

12:36 Passports are confiscated; to be free you buy yourself back
The source, using the name Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India who was lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, covering the cost of bringing him over plus food and lodging, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions from scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not the chains-and-beatings kind of prison, but is packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next client like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

14:40 Fines are more reliable than wages
Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for missing contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the con — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, committing deeply destructive crimes.

15:45 Video calls run on a dedicated face-swap model
Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish their language, never run out of graceful phrasing, even write little motivational poems and find the exactly right goodnight line. More crucial is video: the boss instructed them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible and stall with excuses; when stalling failed, the compound had a dedicated room and a model whose full-time job was video calls, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this kind of software is not perfect, but by the video-call stage the victim wants so badly to believe it is real that they overlook the flaws.

18:54 The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
Greenberg's judgment is that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already beginning to appear — is fully autonomous AI fraud. He cites a case from an Anthropic report the previous week: a Chinese group built 20 dating apps populated entirely by AI, where victims had to keep paying to continue the conversation, and "most" of the other side were fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that at most stages of the scam process, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more invested, more attentive — which is exactly what the con is doing for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

23:08 Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months that Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but Laos alone has dozens of such compounds, and Cambodia and Myanmar have more, and together they add up to the billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," so he was penniless, eating only the compound canteen's rice and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

24:12 Forging a police letter to escape, then beaten when caught
Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home state in India, saying he was under investigation and had to return to deal with it or his boss would also be in trouble. Greenberg advised him not to do it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately detected. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant, to make him talk more, while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

item.title: Entropy Increasing Doesn't Mean Things Getting Messy: Oil and Water Separating, Frost Crystals Forming Are All Spontaneous Order
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-intotheimpossi-熵增不等于变乱-油水分层-霜花结晶都是自发的秩序/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-intotheimpossi-熵增不等于变乱-油水分层-霜花结晶都是自发的秩序/
item.category: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating
item.description: The second law of thermodynamics is often told as "things get messier and messier," but oil separating from water, beach sorting, and frost flowers on a window are all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe, but in the way we look at the universe.
item.content:encoded:
The second law of thermodynamics is often told as "things get messier and messier," but oil separating from water, beach sorting, and frost flowers on a window are all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe, but in the way we look at the universe.

This episode has medium-to-high information density. The first half, on entropy and time, is the most valuable; the second half, on AI and free will, is more speculative. The ad segment can be skipped.

2:03 Oil separating from water isn't anti-entropy; it's entropy producing order
Rovelli uses a set of everyday images to dismantle the popular claim that "entropy = disorder": water and vinegar mix into a uniform blend, but water and oil separate into layers after mixing; on a beach, fine sand and pebbles sort themselves apart; frost on a window spontaneously grows regular structures. He says that under a properly defined "order," many things in nature become spontaneously ordered when left alone. This does not overturn the second law; it says popular science draws the correspondence between "order" and "entropy" too crudely. He specifically points out that the complexity of biology and the structure of the Earth's surface are often misread as "anti-entropy," when in fact entropy growth itself is constantly producing order.

7:12 Low entropy may not be in the universe, but in how you coarse-grain
Rovelli proposes a hypothesis he has put into a paper himself but is not sure is right or wrong: low entropy means "special," but what is special is not the state of the universe, but coarse graining itself. Coarse graining is a perspective — looking only at some variables, not all the details. If this hypothesis holds, the universe can be in a completely arbitrary state, but from our perspective, which sees only some variables, it appears low-entropy in the direction we call "the past." This turns the "initial low-entropy boundary condition" from a fact about the universe into a question about how observers partition information.

12:16 You can be in two places at once, just not to yourself
Rovelli pushes quantum superposition onto people: if quantum mechanics is universal, Brian can be in a superposition of Los Angeles and San Francisco, and to Carlo this interference can be measured. But to Brian himself, quantum mechanics never tells you that you are in a superposition — you look around and see either San Diego or Los Angeles. So "where you are" is two different things for you and for me. He compares this to Galileo discovering that velocity is relative: saying "velocity is zero" actually omits "relative to the Earth." What quantum mechanics says is that all properties must be understood relative to something.

19:34 Galileo used the principle of relativity and got the tides wrong
Rovelli uses Galileo's tidal model to show that "having an idea" and "pushing the idea to the end" are two different things. Galileo thought the combination of the Earth's revolution around the Sun plus its rotation stirred the seas and produced the tides. But Rovelli points out that revolution is, to first order, uniform straight-line motion, and rotation alone cannot produce an effect either, so the tides cannot come from this — what actually explains the tides is Newton. Galileo himself precisely violated the principle of relativity he had discovered. Rovelli says Einstein was the same: after writing general relativity in 1915, he later wrote a paper denying gravitational waves (and corrected it after a referee sent it back), and also insisted that the Schwarzschild singularity was the end of the world, an error he never corrected until his death.

31:06 Without dissipation you can't record anything
Rovelli says that already in classical mechanics he found a fact that made him "see the light": if you want to model a measuring device with classical mechanics — a barometer, say, or a device that records whether a ball is on the left or the right — you can't do it unless you introduce dissipation. A ball dropped into a box will bounce back up; it must dissipate in order to stop and leave a record. So measurement is essentially a statistical process requiring dissipation, and this was already true before quantum mechanics; it is not peculiar to quantum mechanics. This directly answers the puzzle of "unitary evolution is reversible, so where does irreversibility come from": recording itself requires that something be thrown away.

33:45 A chess program deliberates, and so do you
Rovelli uses his chess computer to take apart free will: the computer is deterministic, and given its internal state and the opponent's move, its output is necessarily predetermined. But why does it still spend time enumerating all possible moves and evaluating them one by one? Because the only way to reach that result is to go through this evaluation process, and that process is called deliberation. He says it would be foolish to say it is not deliberating, because deliberation is exactly this. Brian is the same: if he did not go through this complex process, he would not make the decision to start a project or choose a career. So-called freedom is not violating the laws of nature; it is precisely the fact of "having gone through deliberation" itself.

40:56 In principle yes, not now, and within two years he doubts it
Asked whether machines could have Einstein's "happiest thought" (the equivalence principle in free fall), Rovelli answers in three layers: in principle yes, he does not think humans are so special as to be unreproducible; not now; and within two years he is skeptical, but has no hard evidence that it is impossible. He mentions that last week he had Claude do something his PhD student had not finished in a month, and Claude finished it in half an hour, so the capability is beyond doubt. But he says Claude did not invent the equivalence principle, and doing that within two years he finds hard. At the same time he states plainly that there is a lot of hype in AI.

56:45 Ten years and unlimited funding, he'd build a roomful of Josephson junctions
Asked what he would do with "ten years and unlimited funding," Rovelli's answer is not a telescope or a collider, but a large room filled with Josephson junctions, plus an engineering team. The reason: loop quantum gravity predicts particles of Planck mass, which could be dark matter candidates, with a mass roughly equal to a small piece of hair or a flea egg. He says we already know the direction, mass, and interaction strength of dark matter clouds; although it is only an extremely weak Newtonian gravity, Josephson junctions could catch it with simple physics. He thinks it is technically feasible within ten years, and what is missing is only money.

item.title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Blocker Was the Engine, Not Aerodynamics

item.description: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because its sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because its sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.

The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting into data-center power generation, with concrete numbers and regulatory detail, at high information density.

5:12 Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
Boom's answer to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls this boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff. The boom is still produced by the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York landing in San Francisco at 9:30 still holds. Over the ocean no one is listening, so full speed is fine. Push the logic to its limit and you get the line: if there is no boom at all, there is nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
The U.S. ban on overland supersonic flight, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order could in theory be reversed by the next person, so he turned to pushing legislation through Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic is not a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, Boom split publicly with Rolls-Royce, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch themselves — and not just design it, but manufacture even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, in-house. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at high temperature, full power, for long periods at Mach 1.7, with the fan removed from the front and a generator bolted on the back, is a power-generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application is not in the sky but on the ground. Take off the fan, swap in a generator at the back, put it in a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake pointed out specifically that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial point of this path: before the supersonic airliner gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it is selling to the buyer with the least shortage of money right now.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom putting the engine to work in ground power generation first has an engineering side effect: this will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success is not guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine's validation comes from accumulating flight hours, and Boom has moved validation onto the ground and into data-center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test bill for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, with the actual price likely higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom intends to take all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he says explicitly that ‘fast matters more than predictable’, cannot give a firm date, and only commits to delivering at the earliest time physically possible — from the outside that looks like around 2030. There is a trade-off worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it is unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data-center demand is so large they plan to auction it
Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and he says his inbox holds tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine will fire up next month, and then they intend to auction off all of the capacity. Asked whether he has talked to Elon, or whether this is for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is that it gives an anomalous supply-demand signal: for a power product not yet in mass production, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has shifted from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake recaps how fast this regulatory push moved: broke the sound barrier on a Monday, tweeted, Elon retweeted, flew to Washington that night to start lobbying for legalization, and by the time he landed had an invitation from the White House; into the West Wing on Tuesday, and by Thursday the aircraft model was in the Oval Office — and it is still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow but concedes would be slower under another administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a single technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.

item.title: Why rebranding a charity is more dangerous than rebranding a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
